{{Short description|British astronomer and mathematician}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2025}}
{{Use British English|date=September 2015}}
'''Lawrence Rooke''' (also Laurence) (1622&ndash;26 June 1662) was an English [[astronomer]] and [[mathematician]]. He was also one of the founders of the [[Royal Society]], although he died as it was being formally constituted.

==Life==
He was born in [[Deptford]], and was a great-nephew through his mother of [[Lancelot Andrewes]].<ref name = Ronan>C. A. Ronan, ''Laurence Rooke (1622&ndash;1662)'', Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London, Vol. 15, (Jul. 1960), pp. 113&ndash;118.</ref>

He was educated at [[Eton College]] and [[King's College, Cambridge]], where he graduated M.A. in 1647.<ref>{{acad|id=RK640L|name=Rooke, Lawrence}}</ref> He became a fellow commoner at [[Wadham College, Oxford]] in 1650, having dropped out of academia for a period because of bad health.<ref name = CDNB>''Concise Dictionary of National Biography''</ref><ref name = Pyle>[[Andrew Pyle (philosopher)|Andrew Pyle]] (editor), ''Dictionary of Seventeenth Century British Philosophers'' (2000), p. 691.</ref> At Wadham he worked closely with [[John Wilkins]] and [[Seth Ward (bishop)|Seth Ward]].<ref name = Ronan/>

He became Professor of Astronomy at [[Gresham College]] in 1652, and then [[Gresham Professor of Geometry|Professor of Geometry]] there, in 1657, an appointment in which [[Oliver Cromwell]] took an interest.<ref name = CDNB/><ref>[[Christopher Hill (historian)|Christopher Hill]], ''[[God's Englishman]]'' (1972 edition), pp. 250&ndash;1.</ref>

He was unpublished in his lifetime, but left papers on [[longitude]] and the [[moons of Jupiter]] that were published posthumously. He also wrote at the Royal Society's request a set of directions for sailors, on the correct way to record meteorological and oceanographic observations on their travels. These appeared in volume 1 of the Royal Society's ''Philosophical Transactions'' as ''Directions for Sea-men, bound for far Voyages'' (Phil. Trans. 1665 1 140–143) [http://rstl.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/1/1-22/140.full.pdf+html doi:10.1098/rstl.1665.0066].<ref>Michael McKeon, ''The Origins of the English Novel, 1600&ndash;1740'' (2002), p. 102.</ref>

[[Montes Rook]], a circular mountain range on the moon, is named after Lawrence Rooke.
